content.title: Choice of privacy parameter using utility
content.review:
The paper gives a new way to estimate the privacy parameter $\epsilon$ given a utility guarantee that a user is looking for.  Choosing the privacy parameter is one of the basic problems in the implementation of differentially private algorithms and only a small number of work shed any light on it. The paper analyzes one of the earlier algorithm for privacy preserving learning that uses objective perturbation. 

The assumptions made in the paper is reasonable: the loss function is twice differentiable. The paper claims that if the function is non-differentiable, we can approximate it with the one that is twice differentiable; however, that would incur some more utility loss. The authors do not give any rigorous reason as to why it is always possible. 

There is a something else that I do not understand in the paper. Theorem 3 makes an assumption on the boundedness of gradient, Hessian, the high dimensional variant of torsion (third order derivative) is bounded. The norm is not clear to me. Is the spectral norm of the Hessian is bounded and what is the norm of torsion that the authors assume is bounded? Secondly, what is the equivalent of that in the geometry of function is not clear to me. This makes their claim on the approximate case a little hard to understand. 

If I understand correctly, the technique would only work when $\epsilon$ is small because of Taylor's approximation. Can we use Analytic methods to estimate $\epsilon$ in other cases? I am guessing there would be some numerical stability issues in the naive algorithm that tries to estimate privacy parameter using Analytic method. I am raising this question because in practice, we often have $\epsilon \geq 1$ and not less than $1!$.

Last point is a general question: why does the author consider unconstrained setting? We know there is a difference between utility guarantees achievable in constrained vs unconstained setting in the regime of PPML.
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Thanks for your comments.
content.comment:
**Comment-1:** The assumptions made in the paper is reasonable: the loss function is twice differentiable. The paper claims that if the function is non-differentiable, we can approximate it with the one that is twice differentiable; however, that would incur some more utility loss. The authors do not give any rigorous reason as to why it is always possible.
* **Response:** Thanks for your comment. As the reviewer said, the assumptions are reasonable as most common loss functions (such as Mean Square Error, Huber Loss, Cross-entropy loss, etc) are twice differentiable. By saying to approximate the non-differentiable function, we mean that we can swap out non-differentiable components for smoothed versions of function. This can be easily done in general cases. As for the utility loss, this is inevitable. However, since most common loss functions are twice differentiable, we did not do much analysis on it in this paper. In the future work, we may further relax the restrictions on the loss function for our method. We have revised the relevant misleading descriptions in the revision.

**Comment-3:** If I understand correctly, the technique would only work when $\epsilon$ is small because of Taylor's approximation. Can we use Analytic methods to estimate $\epsilon$ in other cases? I am guessing there would be some numerical stability issues in the naive algorithm that tries to estimate privacy parameter using Analytic method. I am raising this question because in practice, we often have $\epsilon \ge 1$ and not less than $1$.
* **Response:** Thanks for your comment. Due to Equation 16, we have that our error bound is  inversely proportional to the value of measuring $\epsilon$. That is, our method can also be used in the case of larger $\epsilon$ values, and can achieve better accuracy. The reason why we limit $\epsilon$ to less than 1 in Theorem 3 is that this makes it easier to bound $\delta$, however, due to Equation 4 we also have that $\delta = 0$ when $\epsilon$ is set to be large. Thus, our method can be applied to the case with larger $\epsilon$. Even so, we would suggest not going beyond $\epsilon = 1$ for all differential privacy mechanisms, as this gives a meaningless privacy guarantee in practice.

**Comment-4:** Why does the author consider unconstrained setting? We know there is a difference between utility guarantees achievable in constrained vs unconstained setting in the regime of PPML.
* **Response:** Thanks for your comment. As a new attempt in this field, the focus of this article is to verify the effectiveness of our method on differentially private machine learning, thus the unconstrained setting is our best choice for the first step. We will explore the way to generalize the approximation scheme to the constrained setting and compare the difference between them in our future work.

content.title: Review for paper #235
content.review:
The paper considers the problem of how to select the privacy parameter $\epsilon$ for differentially private empirical risk minimization, which is of broad interest to the community. The paper approaches the problem by providing an approximation scheme for the empirical error under different $\epsilon$ based on computations under a fixed $\epsilon_0$. With the approximation, the trainer can select the privacy level based on the anticipated utility. The paper considers the objective perturbation scheme proposed in Chaudhuri et al 2011 and the approximation is based on the Taylor expansion of the empirical error with respect to $\epsilon$ at point $\epsilon = \epsilon_0$. The paper also conducts experiments on various datasets to show that the approximation scheme is accurate with an okay error.

My main critique of the paper is that the approximation scheme is not private. To be exact, the approximation formula (equation 9 in the paper) is based on non-private statistics of the dataset (e.g. the gradient of the empirical loss with respect to $\theta$), which makes the choice of the new $\epsilon'$ not private and neither is the final output because of composition. This makes the theory of the paper unsolid. So the paper is a clear reject from my side.

Other comments:
1. The paper only considers pure DP while approximate DP is the more interesting case in practice. It is not clear how this can be generalized to the approximate DP case.
2. In the paper, it is stated that the "user" can select the privacy parameter. It is worth pointing out that this user is not the data contributors whose privacy the scheme is protecting. The "user" in the paper is referring to the "learner", which makes the motivation of the method less convincing.

Minor comments:
1. Page 1: results in useless model ---> results in a useless model.
2. Page 1: too small $\epsilon$ may lose to much utility ---> too much utility
3. Page 5: formular ---> formula.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.comment:
I guess you mean that the item $\nabla_{\theta}L(\hat{\theta}_{\epsilon}, D)$ is non-private. However, this term is calculated with the final private parameters, which makes it a private statistic. 

Besides, there is one more thing I need to clarify. The privacy concerns of machine learning mechanisms generally refer to the privacy threats of the released model. More concretely, when sensitive data is used to train the machine learning model, the model itself might unwittingly leak information about that data through either their behavior (i.e., black-box attack [1-3]) or the details of their structure (i.e., white-box attack [4-6]). As a temporary calculation result of searching for the optimal $\epsilon$, the terms and results of Equation 9 will not be released to the public, only the model trained with that $\epsilon$ will be released finally, which is private as required. Your concerns are reasonable, but is not the focus of this paper.


==================================

References
[1]. Daniel Lowd and Christopher Meek. Adversarial learning. In ACM SIGKDD, 2005.
[2]. Reza Shokri, Marco Stronati, Congzheng Song, and Vitaly Shmatikov. Membership inference attacks against machine learning models. In IEEE S&P, 2017.

content.title: This is not a reasonable privacy concern.
content.comment:
I strongly disagree with your point for the following three reasons. 

* First of all, it is not necessary for the user to release the privacy parameters with the final model, and releasing only the model will not disclose the choice of privacy parameters. 
* Secondly, our method only provides a more efficient way to find the optimal $\epsilon$ rather than determining its value. There is no direct connection between whether to use our method to find the optimal $\epsilon$ and whether it reveal private information.
* Thirdly, due to the randomness of added noise, I don't think the privacy parameters can really reveal some private information.

display_title: This is a real privacy concern.

content.title: This is a real privacy concern.
content.comment:
We can think of the final release information as the following mapping:
$\lambda(D) = f(D, \epsilon(D))$ since $\epsilon(D)$ also depends on the data. To use composition to argue that  $\lambda(D)$ is private, we need both $f(D, \cdot)$ and $\epsilon(D)$ to be differentially private no matter of whether we release $\epsilon(D)$ or not. 

This being said, it is possible that if you don't release $\epsilon(D)$, you can get certain (or better) privacy guarantees compared to using composition, e.g. in [1]. But you need to prove it rigorous before claiming it. 

[1] Privacy Amplification by Iteration. Vitaly Feldman, Ilya Mironov, Kunal Talwar, Abhradeep Thakurta

display_title: care with privacy parameters computed from the data

content.title: care with privacy parameters computed from the data
content.comment: Even if the privacy parameter is not output, it determines the amount of noise added to compute the model. Adding more noise will result in a different distribution on the final model, and an adversary  can use this to try to infer what the privacy parameter is. This is easier to see with something simpler, like adding Laplace noise to a count: if the private information consists of a bit belonging to each person, and the adversary knows everyone's bit but mine (the standard attack model in differential privacy), then the adversary can determine the sum of my bit and the noise. If this value is large, then it's more likely that epsilon was small. If epsilon was chosen based on the private data, this is a problem.

content.title: Maybe you have some misunderstanding about our method
content.comment:
I think an example would be helpful to address your issues. Before that, let me first reiterate that our method (as well as other method for choosing $\epsilon$) is to find the $\epsilon$ that provides optimal utility-privacy trade-off.

Given a training dataset, a differential private learning method and the expected utility of the final model. Suppose $0.3$ is the minimum value of $\epsilon$ that can satisfy the expected utility (i.e. if $\epsilon < 0.3$, the utility will be lower than expected). We say that $0.3$ is the optimal value of $\epsilon$, because it can provide the maximum privacy guarantee with the satisfactory utility. The goal of our method (as well as other methods for choosing $\epsilon$) is to find $0.3$. To use our method, one should first start with an arbitrary point, let's say $\epsilon=0.7$, as the measuring point to train a private model. Then, the gap between the utility of that model and the expected utility can be obtained. Finally, the optimal choice of $\epsilon$ can be calculated by Equation 9 (the result may be near $0.3$ due to the loss of accuracy). If one uses the traditional method, he/she may try many times (i.e. $\epsilon=0.7, 0.6, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3$) to reach to the optimal $\epsilon$, that each attempt requires training of the model. In the end, the user will release the private model trained with $\epsilon=0.3$, no matter the $\epsilon$ value is found by our method or other methods.

I hope the above example would address your concerns.

replying_to: Replying to Maybe you have some misunderstanding about our method

content.title: Privacy guarantee of multiple trails
content.comment:
If you fix $\epsilon$ independent of data and run an $\epsilon$-DP algorithm, your output is private. However, if you select $\epsilon$ based on your data (denoted as $\eps(D)$) and run an $\epsilon(D)$-DP algorithm, your output is not $\epsilon(D)$ private, it might be private, but it depends on how private your $\epsilon(D)$ is. 

For example, if you try different $\epsilon$'s, e.g $\epsilon = 0.3, 0.7, 0.9$ and select the one giving the best tradeoff (assume it is 0.7) and output the parameter. Then your output is not 0.7-DP. It is 0.3+0.7+0.9 = 1.9-DP if you use naive composition (you may get better parameters if you consider more advanced composition techniques.) 

These being said, the algorithm you proposed to choose $\epsilon(D)$ is not trivially private. So it doesn't imply the final output is private even if you run an $\epsilon(D)$-DP algorithm afterward because they can extract information from the $\epsilon(D)$ you use. Reviewer 4 gives a good example of this:
https://openreview.net/forum?id=Xu6K3lGBPAS&noteId=6M5dt6wEf_

content.comment:
I think it may help to clear up the misunderstanding between us by reiterating our threat model.

There are two roles in our threat model, which are the user and the adversary. The user tries to learn and release a model from the data he/she owns, and the adversary tries to infer the sensitive information from the released model. Thus, the user must ensure that the released model is secure enough to resist attacks from the adversary, and at the same time satisfies others' requirements of utility (who are going to use that model). The user must choose $\epsilon$ carefully. However, since the adversary can only obtain the released model (maybe the value of $\epsilon$ as well), the user can find the most suitable $\epsilon$ in a secure environment by various means (including our method). After $\epsilon$ is determined, the user trains the final model with that value and release them to the public (including the adversary).

Thus, we think, the process of finding optimal $\epsilon$ will not involve the privacy concerns as reviewer1 and reviewer4 said. For example,  after I try different $\epsilon$'s, e.g $\epsilon=0.3,0.7,0.9$ and select the one giving the best tradeoff (assume it is 0.7) and output the parameter, I will only release the model trained with $\epsilon=0.7$, and the adversary can not obtain the model trained by the other two $\epsilon$. Then, I think the model is exactly 0.7-DP, not 1.9-DP for the adversary.

This thread model is widely studied in DPML, such as [1-6].

===============================================

References 

[1]. Daniel Lowd and Christopher Meek. Adversarial learning. In ACM SIGKDD, 2005. 

[2]. Reza Shokri, Marco Stronati, Congzheng Song, and Vitaly Shmatikov. Membership inference attacks against machine learning models. In IEEE S&P, 2017. 

[3]. Florian Tramèr, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels, Michael K Reiter, and Thomas Ristenpart. Stealing machine learning models via prediction apis. In USENIX Security, 2016. 

[4]. Giuseppe Ateniese, Giovanni Felici, Luigi V Mancini, Angelo Spognardi, Antonio Villani, and Domenico Vitali. Hacking smart machines with smarter ones: How to extract meaningful data from machine learning classifiers. From arXiv:1306.4447, 2013. 

[5]. Karan Ganju, Qi Wang, Wei Yang, Carl A Gunter, and Nikita Borisov. Property inference attacks on fully connected neural networks using permutation invariant representations. In ACM CCS, 2018. 

[6]. Samuel Yeom, Irene Giacomelli, Matt Fredrikson, and Somesh Jha. Privacy risk in machine learning: Analyzing the connection to overfitting. In IEEE CSF, 2018.

display_title: The privacy concern about selecting the privacy parameter based on data

content.title: The privacy concern about selecting the privacy parameter based on data
content.comment: Differential privacy is a strong privacy notion such that even if the adversary knows the exact algorithm, the algorithm also provides a privacy guarantee about the data. Consider the two algorithms: (a) fix $\epsilon = 0.7$ and output the model obtained under this parameter and (b) obtain models under $\epsilon = 0.3, 0.7, 0.9$ and output the one that has the best tradeoff. For algorithm (b) the fact that the model with $\epsilon = 0.7$ is output tells us information about the model obtained under $\epsilon = 0.3, 0.9$. In other words, the output distribution of the parameters is no the same as algorithm (a) even conditioned on the event that you output the model obtained under $\epsilon = 0.7$ because it is conditional distribution. Hence it is not true to claim that algorithm (b) has the same privacy guarantee as algorithm (a).

replying_to: Replying to The privacy concern about selecting the privacy parameter based on data

content.title: confused about difference between (a) and (b)
content.comment: Honestly speaking, I don't see the difference between (a) and (b). In my view, when $\epsilon = \epsilon'$, the objective function would be the same, thus, why does the same function train on the same dataset will result in different parameters? More concretely, when $\epsilon$ is fixed, $\beta_{\epsilon}$ and $\delta_{\epsilon}$ in Equation 4 is determined as well as the Equation 2. If you don't know how $\epsilon$ is determined, then will there be any difference in the privacy guarantee of the models obtained by two independent training with the same $\epsilon$? From the perspective of the user, the privacy guarantee may be different as he/she knows everything, but from the perspective of the adversary, the training process (including optimal $\epsilon$ selection) is a black-box. He could not know how the user chooses the $\epsilon$, but only get the final model and its $\epsilon$. Thus, I think, the privacy guarantee of (a) is the same of (b) to the adversary.

content.title: One more example.
content.comment:
Let me give you one more example. I believe you are claiming the privacy guarantee the following proposed scheme:

(1) There is a family of learning algorithms $f_{\epsilon}: D \rightarrow \theta, \forall \epsilon > 0$. And $\forall \epsilon, f_{\epsilon}(D)$ is $\epsilon$-DP. In the paper, these are objective perturbation with different level of noises.

(2) There is an algorithm to choose $\epsilon(D)$, which is a function of $D$, based on previous discussion between us, $\epsilon(D)$ may not be private.

https://openreview.net/forum?id=Xu6K3lGBPAS&noteId=0d120iDoVE3

(3) The final output is $f_{\epsilon(D)} (D)$.

And you are claiming $f_{\epsilon(D)} (D)$ is $\epsilon(D)$-DP.

Here is a concrete example of why this is not true:
Let $f_{\epsilon} (D) = \epsilon$, then $f_{\epsilon} (D)$ is perfectly private since the output doesn't depend on $D$ at all. So $f_{\epsilon} (D)$ is  $\epsilon$-DP, for all $\epsilon$. 

Now the output of the proposed selecting approach will be $f_{\epsilon(D)} (D) = \epsilon(D)$. Hence it has the same privacy guarantee as  $\epsilon(D)$, which has not been proved to be private in the submission. 

The intuition is that although $f_{\epsilon} (D)$ may be private about $D$, the choice of $\epsilon(D)$ may still leak information about the users' date $D$, which may further be leaked through the final output $f_{\epsilon(D)} (D)$.

I hope this example explains why the privacy claim in the submission is not solid.

replying_to: Replying to One more example.

content.title: Concerns about choosing epsilon
content.comment:
I understand your example, but I don't think it supports your point. However, at this time, I will try to start from your point to see what's wrong with it. 

The first is my conclusion. If the reviewer is right, then choosing optimal $\epsilon$ for DPML is meaningless since it may leak privacy. The effect of $\epsilon$ on utility is inherent, that is, there always exists a function that can express this relationship or mapping (an approximation  is already given by our method). It doesn't mean that this relationship will not exist if you find the optimal $\epsilon$ by other methods (such as trying $\epsilon$ one by one). Your point is not that our method may leak privacy, but is that this inherent relationship may leak privacy, which is caused by DPML itself. Although this possibility exists (for all methods), I don't think it's a real threat because there's too much randomness in it. 

Besides, there are many simple ways to solve your concerns. For example, you can randomly choose a neighbor point near the optimal one found by our method, which may have a little more accuracy loss. 

Finally, I must reiterate that our method only finds a better fitting function to fit the relationship between $\epsilon$ and utility, so that we can deduce $\epsilon$ from utility more efficiently. Just as the reviewer says, there are some characteristics of data implied in this relationship. But even if you don't choose $\epsilon$ by any method, the adversary can still use this relationship to infer privacy information after obtaining the model, model utility and $\epsilon$ you used (in fact, what the adversary can obtain in our paper is also these 3 items), if your claims are correct.

replying_to: Replying to Concerns about choosing epsilon

content.title: Choosing epsilon based on data.
content.comment:
Most of the algorithms in DPML need to assume that $\epsilon$ is not selected based on data.  You are right, the process that selecting $\epsilon$ based on multiple trials may not be private if the selection process doesn't guarantee that. All I am trying to say is that if the $\epsilon$ used for the algorithm is selected as a function based on the data $D$, then the selection process needs to be private as well to make the final output private.

These being said, I agree there is still randomness in the process, so the algorithm might have some privacy guarantee. However, it is not rigorously proved in the paper. For a DP paper, it is important to prove rigorously that the process is private. 

And I agree that adding noise in the selection process might guarantee privacy if proved rigorously. It would be great if this issue can be resolved in future modifications of the work. However, I cannot see how to obtain a private algorithm easily from the submitted manuscript.

Regarding your last point, any algorithm that depends on data will leak information about the data. However, any rigorously proved DP algorithm will guarantee that the amount of information leaked from any individual data point is small.

content.title: Post-processing vs Composition
content.comment:
We need to distinguish between post-processing and composition. 

Post-processing: $f(g(D))$ is $\epsilon$-DP about $D$ as long as $g(D)$ is $\epsilon$-DP about $D$, given $f$ has no access to $D$.

Composition: $f(D,  g(D))$ is $\epsilon_1 + \epsilon_2$-DP about $D$ if $g(D)$ is $\epsilon_1$-DP and $f(D, \cdot)$ is $\epsilon_2$-DP. Clearnly, $\nabla_{\theta} L(\theta_\epsilon, D)$ has access to $D$. So post-processing won't work here. You need to use composition property of DP and $\epsilon_2$ here is infinity. So the I don't think the approximation step is private, as least it is not easy to see.

content.title: Review
content.review:
The paper mainly study the problem that, for DP-ERM, how to choose the appropriate $\epsilon$. By using the objective perturbation method and calculating the partial derivative of the perturbed function w.r.t $\epsilon$, the authors get a closed form solution to approximate  $\hart{\theta}_{\epsilon'}$, giving the parameter $\hart{\theta}_{\epsilon}$ and $\epsilon$. That is, we can predict the performance when the privacy budget is $\epsilon'$ for any $\epsilon'$ if we just know $\hart{\theta}_{\epsilon}$ for a fixed $\epsilon$. Thus, we can select the best privacy budget. 

However, I tend to reject due to the following reasons. 

1. The method of this paper heavily depends on the objective perturbation method. However, as we know, objective perturbation method only holds for some convex loss function (that is with additional assumptions), it does not hold for non-convex loss. Thus, I think the generalization of the method in this paper is limited. 

2. Theorem 3 needs too many assumptions so that I think it cannot be used to many loss functions.

**Comment-1:** The method of this paper heavily depends on the objective perturbation method. However, as we know, objective perturbation method only holds for some convex loss function (that is with additional assumptions), it does not hold for non-convex loss. Thus, I think the generalization of the method in this paper is limited.
* **Response:** Thanks for your comment. We focus our attention on the technique of objective perturbation, because prior works (such as [1-3]) as well as our own preliminary empirical results have hinted at its superior performance on convex optimization. In this paper, we aim to verifying the effectiveness and feasibility of this method on differentially private machine learning, and we consider extending our method to other mechanism, such as gradient perturbation, to address more general issues in our future work.

=========================

Reference

[1]. K. Chaudhuri, C. Monteleoni, and A. D. Sarwate. Differentially private empirical risk minimization. In JMLR, 2011.

content.title: Interesting idea, but not convinced approach is useful. Some correctness issues and missing references
content.review:
### Summary

The authors propose a method to estimate the loss of a model trained with the differentially private objective perturbation method at many values of the privacy parameter epsilon, without retraining for each value of epsilon. The method is to train the model for one value of epsilon, and to use a first order Taylor approximation for nearby values of epsilon. 

### Evaluation

The authors’ claim that this is the first paper to propose choosing epsilon based on utility is incorrect. In fact this is the method of choice in deployed differentially private systems, as far as I know. Methods for choosing a value of epsilon based on utility without rerunning mechanisms from scratch have been proposed before as well, for example the noise reduction method from “Accuracy First: Selecting a Differential Privacy Level for Accuracy-Constrained ERM” by Ligett et al.

Having more ideas in this space is valuable. The method proposed, being just a first order Taylor expansion, unfortunately only applies to values of epsilon that are very close to the one the model was trained on. Usually there would be enough uncertainty about the performance of the model with different values of epsilon that one would want to try values that are spread out. Because of that, it does not seem to me that the method the authors propose will be useful in most typical applications.

There are also a few places where I am not convinced the mathematics are correct:

* Equation (4) fails to specify the assumptions on the loss from the Chaudhuri et al paper. One needs the losses to satisfy some bounds on the first and second derivatives. Without this, it’s not clear what the parameter $c$ is, for example.

* The derivative of $b_\epsilon$ with respect to $\epsilon$ is not generally defined. Later on it becomes clear that the authors fix a map from random samples in the unit interval to $b_{\epsilon}$ and this map is differentiable for fixed randomness. This is reasonable, but should be clarified before the statement of Theorem 1.

* The derivations in Section 4.2 are incorrect. The expression in (11) is the CDF of the Laplace distribution, so the distribution for $b_\epsilon$ that the authors are sampling is IID Laplace random variables. But the density in (3), and in Chaudhuri et al, is not that of the Laplace distribution: rather, it’s exponential in the $\ell_2$ norm. 

A final remark is to be more careful with references. Why is the reference for the Taylor expansion some 1976 paper rather than a standard textbook? Why is the Dwork and Roth book listed with “et al” in the author list in the references, when there is no other author? Why is the definition of differential privacy, due to Dwork, McSherry, Nissim, and Smith, attributed only to Dwork?
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: Thanks for the comments.
content.comment:
**Comment-1:** The authors’ claim that this is the first paper to propose choosing $\epsilon$ based on utility is incorrect. In fact this is the method of choice in deployed differentially private systems, as far as I know. Methods for choosing a value of $\epsilon$ based on utility without rerunning mechanisms from scratch have been proposed before as well, for example the noise reduction method from “Accuracy First: Selecting a Differential Privacy Level for Accuracy-Constrained ERM” by Ligett et al.
* **Response:** Thanks for your comment. The original intention of the claim is that we are the first to provide a solution for choosing $\epsilon$ by mathematically estimating (not actually measuring) the influence of $\epsilon$ on utility. As we mentioned at the beginning, most existing methods try the value of $\epsilon$ one by one to seek for the optimal $\epsilon$ (the noise reduction method mentioned by the reviewer is also such a method), which requires a lot of training. However, our method can estimate the utility of various $\epsilon$ values by mathematical calculation, which is much more efficient. We give a detailed comparison between the noise reduction method and our work and have revised some descriptions to reduce misunderstanding in the revision.

**Comment-2:** The method proposed, being just a first order Taylor expansion, unfortunately only applies to values of $\epsilon$ that are very close to the one the model was trained on. Usually there would be enough uncertainty about the performance of the model with different values of $\epsilon$ that one would want to try values that are spread out. Because of that, it does not seem to me that the method the authors propose will be useful in most typical applications.
* **Response:** The reviewer has raised an important point. Due to the use of first order Taylor expansion, our method provides more accurate estimates on adjacent points of the measuring point. But that doesn't mean that our method will be not useful in typical applications. For example, when the user has extremely strict requirements on the estimation accuracy, he/she can initialize several dispersed measuring points so that the measuring point closer to the target point can be selected. By using the estimation method after that, we can efficiently obtain the utility value of a large number of points to help us to find the optimal value of $\epsilon$. Another example is that, when the utility expectation of a well-trained private model changes, the user can use our method to directly obtain the value of $\epsilon$ satisfying the new expectation, without retraining the model.

**Comment-3:** Equation (4) fails to specify the assumptions on the loss from the Chaudhuri et al paper. One needs the losses to satisfy some bounds on the first and second derivatives. Without this, it’s not clear what the parameter $\epsilon$ is, for example.
* **Response:** Thanks for pointing out our mistakes. We have fixed this issue in the revision.

**Comment-4:** The derivative of $b_{\epsilon}$ with respect to $\epsilon$ is not generally defined. Later on it becomes clear that the authors fix a map from random samples in the unit interval to $b_{\epsilon}$ and this map is differentiable for fixed randomness. This is reasonable, but should be clarified before the statement of Theorem 1.
* **Response:** Thanks for your comment. In fact, it is difficult to define the derivative of $b_{\epsilon}$ with respect to $\epsilon$ exactly. We only provide a method for calculating the derivative of $b_{\epsilon}$ with respect to $\epsilon$ in Section 4.2, which we think is better after the statement of Theorem 1.

**Comment-5:** The derivations in Section 4.2 are incorrect. The expression in (11) is the CDF of the Laplace distribution, so the distribution for $b_{\epsilon}$ that the authors are sampling is IID Laplace random variables. But the density in (3), and in Chaudhuri et al, is not that of the Laplace distribution: rather, it’s exponential in $\ell_2$ the norm.
* **Response:** Thanks for your comment. We have carefully re-examined our derivation of (10) and (11) and are convinced that they are correct. It should be emphasized that both (10) and (11) are derived from (3) and the CDF is not specified. The derivation is based on the following two facts: (3) is symmetric with respect to the y-axis and for any probability density function $f(x), \int_{- \infty}^{+ \infty}f(x)dx=1$.

**Comment-6:** A final remark is to be more careful with references. Why is the reference for the Taylor expansion some 1976 paper rather than a standard textbook? Why is the Dwork and Roth book listed with “et al” in the author list in the references, when there is no other author? Why is the definition of differential privacy, due to Dwork, McSherry, Nissim, and Smith, attributed only to Dwork?
* **Response:** Thanks for the comment. We have fixed this issue in the revision.

content.title: noise distributions
content.comment:
The noise may have independent coordinates in these papers, but the noise you define in (3) in **your paper** and the noise in the paper by Chaudhuri et al (see equation (4) in https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume12/chaudhuri11a/chaudhuri11a.pdf) does **not** have independent coordinates. You can see this by the fact that the pdf in (3) cannot be written as the product of functions of the different coordinates. Here I am assuming that the $\\|\cdot\\|$ notation in (3) in your paper means the $\ell_2$ norm, as it does in Chaudhuri et al.

You could use other noise, for example, Laplace noise, but then you would need to redo the privacy analysis from Chaudhuri et al for objective perturbation.
